arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Andrew Pincus argued that illegal tying requires exploiting control over a tying product.
Justice Breyer questioned why a patent holder would seek a patent without expecting price power.
Justice Scalia asked if refuting the presumption equals demonstrating market power.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests whether a patent on a single component legally implies market power for the larger product. Illinois Tool Works seeks to establish this presumption. Independent Ink argues the presumption is legally incorrect.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Illinois Tool Works wants the Court to recognize a patent as evidence of market power for the larger product.
Independent Ink wants the Court to reject the presumption that a component patent implies market power for the whole product.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Illinois Tool Works argues that a patent on a component legally establishes market power for the entire product.
Independent Ink argues that a patent on a component does not legally establish market power for the entire product.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The outcome defines how courts assess market power in patent cases. It determines whether a component patent legally implies control over the entire product market. This standard affects antitrust litigation involving patented goods.
